Neighbourhood on a map is a graph relation; shortest routes and unavoidable transit points are different questions.
Undirected graph; shortest path length plus reachability after deleting a candidate vertex.
Problem 521. Reading a layered map legend (A1)
A map legend translates symbols into properties. One location may have several properties at the same time.

Legend: tree=forest, wavy line=river, double line=road, arch=bridge, square=village, triangle=hill. Cells: A1 has forest, road; A2 has bridge, river; B1 has forest, river, road; B2 has road, village. Cross-domain check: a survey team starts work at 8:00 and works for 2 hour(s) without a break.

A cell satisfies the task only if it has every required attribute. Extra attributes do not disqualify it unless the task says so. For the cross-domain check, finishing time = starting time + duration.
Which cell or cells satisfy all of these conditions: forest, road? Explain by intersecting the clues. Cross-domain check: at what time does the team finish?

1. Convert the requested symbols into the attribute set ['forest', 'road']. 2. Check each cell for every required attribute. 3. The matching set is ['A1', 'B1']. Cross-domain check: 8+2=10, so the team finishes at 10:00.
Map reading often means intersecting clues rather than recognizing one symbol in isolation.
Set model; each cell has an attribute set; return cells whose set is a superset of the required set.
